lesson_title: How Many Must She Sell Before She Smiles? Cost Accounting
hook_text: Vetkoek number 600 pays the stall fee. Number 601 feeds the family.
clip_script: Ma Zondi sells mince-filled vetkoek outside the train station, eighteen rand each. Her granddaughter, busy with grade 12, asks the question that decides whether the stand survives winter: Gogo, how many must you sell each month just to cover yourself? Sort her costs by how they behave. Every vetkoek eats about ten rand of flour, mince, oil and packet — costs that come and go with each one: variable. And every month, sell or starve, the stall fee takes four thousand eight hundred rand — the cost that arrives like the calendar: fixed. So each eighteen-rand vetkoek, after feeding itself, CONTRIBUTES eight rand toward that fee pile. Now one division: four thousand eight hundred of fixed costs, eight rand of contribution — six hundred vetkoek. Number 600 pays off the stall exactly. Number 601 is the first one that feeds the family. Prove it: six hundred sold is ten thousand eight hundred in; ingredients six thousand, stall fee four thousand eight hundred — ten thousand eight hundred out. Zero. That's break-even. And every decision moves the line: mince prices rise and each one eats twelve rand — break-even jumps to eight hundred. She lifts her price to twenty — it falls to four hundred and eighty. A second stand doubles the fee, and doubles the target. One division, and Ma Zondi can test every business decision before she makes it. So can you.
visual_style: A vetkoek stand at first light outside a train station; each sold vetkoek dropping an eight-rand token onto a fee pile that fills a marked jar, the jar clicking full at 600; levers labelled price, mince and stall fee visibly moving a break-even line up and down.
mood: Warm, resourceful, triumphant at the click.
pacing: Gentle setup, rhythmic coin-drop build, sharp division beat, quick lever montage.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and run the break-even machine on any factory a question invents.
